Woodlands semi-detached house on 8,287 sq ft freehold site hits market for $10.8 mil
article:
A freehold semi-detached home along Jalan Bumbong, within the Woodlands Park landed estate, is up for sale via an expression of interest (EOI) exercise with a guide price of $10.8 million.

It sits on an estimated land area of about 8,287 sq ft — likely the largest to have been made available for sale in the area since records started in 1995, based on caveats, said Lee Sze Teck, Huttons Asia’s senior director of data analytics.

The guide price works out to $1,303 psf on the land area.

Huttons noted that given the sizeable land area, the property also offers “strong potential” for a full rebuild or extensive renovation, subject to the relevant authorities’ approval. That may be an attractive proposition for buyers looking to design a bespoke home from ground up, it added.

With seven bedrooms and generous spaces, the house is “very suitable” for multigenerational living, reckoned Aric Lim, group district director at the agency.

Meanwhile, the upcoming redevelopment of the former Kranji Turf Club will bring around 14,000 new homes to the area. Lim expects this to renew interest in landed properties at Woodlands Park.

The property last changed hands in 2022 for $8 million, or $965 psf, going by caveats lodged.

The EOI exercise for the Jalan Bumbong house will close at 4pm on Sept 21.

title: Are Singapore Blue Chips Too Expensive? 3 Stocks to Examine Before You Buy
article:
With the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) hovering near
record highs
, the big question hangs in the air: do you buy now and risk overpaying, or refrain from buying and risk missing the market’s rise?
A rising stock price does not automatically signal a bubble.
What actually matters is whether underlying earnings, dividends, and future growth justify the valuation.
Let’s look past the price charts and test three SGX heavyweights to see if today’s prices are genuinely overinflated or simply worth every dollar.
Before Calling a Stock “Expensive”, Check These 3 Things
Look at the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, price-to-book (P/B), and dividend yield before writing off a stock as too pricey.
Next, compare the stock’s share price against its five- or ten-year averages.
And one last thing: look forward, not just back.
If the company’s set for strong earnings and steady dividend growth, paying up today might make sense after all.
A S$50 stock can easily be cheaper than a S$5 stock if superior earnings power fully backs justified that price.
DBS Group Holdings (SGX: D05): The Stock That Looks Expensive for Good Reason
DBS has been on a remarkable run, with its share price trading near all-time highs – at S$75.84 as of 20 August 2026 – well above its 52-week low of S$49.70.
For the second quarter of 2026 (2Q2026), DBS reported a
record net profit
of S$3.08 billion, up 9% year-on-year (YoY), while total income crossed S$6 billion for the first time.
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), DBS delivered a return on equity (ROE) of 17.5%, showing strong balance sheet efficiency despite shifting interest rates.
Higher earnings have fed straight into shareholder returns.
The board declared a S$0.66 ordinary dividend along with a S$0.15 capital return dividend, up from the S$0.60 per quarter paid through the first three quarters of FY2025.
That strength comes with a premium price tag – the biggest lender currently trades at a P/E ratio of 19.6x, alongside a trailing dividend yield of 4.2%.
Premium businesses deserve premium valuations, provided their earnings keep up.
Singtel (SGX: Z74): The Dividend Favourite
Singtel stands out as a go-to choice for income-focused investors, with its share price trading at S$4.45 (as of 20 August 2026), up 8.3% over the past year.
Investor interest is anchored by strong defensive earnings.
For 1Q2027, underlying net profit grew 21% YoY to S$831 million.
NCS, Optus, Digital InfraCo, and regional associates like Bharti Airtel and Advanced Info Service (AIS) played big roles in this growth.
Singtel raised its total FY2026 payout to S$0.185 per share, comprising S$0.134 in core dividends and S$0.051 in value realisation dividends, marking strong multi-year payout growth.
The core dividend represents an 80% payout of underlying net profit, in line with Singtel’s stated policy of 70% to 90%, while the value realisation dividend is funded by asset recycling and guided at S$0.03 to S$0.06 per share through FY2030.
Following the stock’s recent rally, Singtel trades at a P/E ratio of 21.1x, slightly above its historical mid-cycle averages, with a trailing dividend yield of 4.2%.
While the yield has narrowed as the share price has risen, the earnings behind it have continued to grow.
ST Engineering (SGX: S63): The Growth Stock at a Higher Multiple
ST Engineering has emerged as a premier industrial growth play, with its share price trading at S$10.85 as of 20 August 2026, far above its 52-week low of S$7.54.
For 1H2026, revenue rose 11% YoY to S$6.57 billion, while net profit jumped 27% to S$512 million.
The group secured S$7.6 billion in new contracts during 1H2026, pushing its order book to a record S$35.7 billion, providing multi-year revenue visibility through 2026 and beyond.
It also raised the 2Q2026 interim dividend to S$0.05 per share from S$0.04 a year ago.
On top of that, operating cash flows hit S$960 million.
But there’s a catch.
ST Engineering now trades at a forward P/E ratio of 31x, well above its historical average multiples.
At this valuation, the market doesn’t leave much room for error.
Any slip-up, whether tighter margins, a supply-chain hiccup or a project running behind, could spark a sharp correction in the stock price.
Buy Now or Wait for a Pullback?
Trying to time the perfect entry is tricky, so a better approach is often to buy in slowly with dollar-cost averaging.
By spreading your investments out over time, you ease into the market and avoid going all-in when prices might be high.
If you prefer to wait for a deal, decide in advance what counts as a good price or yield for you.
Then, hold on to your cash and stay patient until the market gives you that opportunity.
What Would Make These Stocks Truly Too Expensive?
Look out for valuations that shoot up way ahead of a company’s real earnings, dividend yields that drop below what you’d get from risk-free bonds, or growth forecasts that are too good to be true.
The biggest risk comes from paying top dollar now, betting on a future that doesn’t pan out, especially if the company’s basic performance starts to slip.
Overpaying for growth that does not show up is the quickest way to turn a supposedly reliable stock into an expensive regret.
Get Smart: Expensive Is Relative
Singapore blue chips
may seem expensive compared to where they traded a few years ago, but evaluating a business on share price alone misses the point.
A company expanding its net profits and dividend payouts can comfortably justify new all-time highs while remaining solid value.
The critical question isn’t whether a stock has risen sharply, but what realistic return you can expect from today’s price.
That’s what separates overextended stocks from quality businesses built to compound.

title: Mapletree Industrial Trust’s CEO Ler Lily to become Mapletree Investments’ group CFO
article:
Ler Lily, the CEO of Mapletree Industrial Trust’s (MINT) manager, will step down from her position on Oct 1.

Ler, who joined MINT on July 22, 2024, will assume a new role as group chief financial officer of Mapletree Investments. The group’s previous CFO, Wendy Koh, left to join Temasek as chief financial officer. She was the CFO-designate since Aug 1 and will assume the role of CFO on Oct 1.

Anand Tze Ming Chandran, who is currently the head of Mapletree Investments’ Asia Pacific data centres, will become the new CEO of MINT’s manager. He will step into his new role on Oct 1.

Units in MINT closed 1 cent higher or 0.52% up at $1.92 on Aug 21.

title: Evergrande saga highlights short-selling risks, says Andrew Left
article:
(Aug 21): Andrew Left, the US short-seller whose early warnings on China Evergrande Group got him banned from trading in Hong Kong, isn’t in a gloating mood.

After the real estate developer’s founder, Hui Ka Yan, and dozens of associates were sentenced in a Chinese court on Thursday, Left said the drawn-out saga only underscores the inherent perils of short selling.

“Evergrande went up roughly 500% after I called it a house of cards,” Left said in a email to Bloomberg. “Being right and being early aren’t the same trade, and a stock can stay irrational longer than anyone’s conviction lasts.”

The founder of Citron Research was fined HK$1.6 million and hit with a five-year trading ban in Hong Kong in 2016 after questioning Evergrande’s financial soundness. The penalty came after Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission accused Left of market misconduct by making “reckless” allegations about Evergrande in a 2012 research report.

Left faces his own legal troubles in the US, where he was found guilty of securities fraud in June. Prosecutors accused him of using explosive social media posts about dozens of companies to influence their shares for quick profits. He is awaiting a post-trial motions hearing in November and sentencing the following month.

Hui was handed a life sentence in Shenzhen court room on Thursday, capping one of the most dramatic downfalls in Chinese corporate history. After a rapid rise, Evergrande defaulted on a massive debt load, while China’s securities regulator later said it had vastly inflated its 2019 and 2020 revenue and profits.

See also: China plans new fiscal support policies amid growth slowdown

A visibly aged Hui, appearing in court with greying hair, was sentenced alongside 56 associates, including his sons Xu Zhijian and Xu Tenghe. His assets will be confiscated, and his companies were fined a combined 15.82 billion yuan.

“The amount involved in the crime is exceptionally large, the circumstances are particularly heinous, exceptionally heavy economic losses have been caused, and the harm to society is extremely grave,” state media outlet Xinhua reported on Thursday.

Before they were delisted last year, Evergrande’s Hong Kong-listed shares had plunged by more than 99% from a 2017 peak. The selloff wiped out about US$50 billion of stock market value.

See also: Yes, the Hong Kong of old is over

Left took no satisfaction in the trial’s outcome.

“For whatever it’s worth, I never wanted a day of prison for Hui, or for anyone,” he said. “Watching that sentence come down wasn’t satisfying.”

title: Singapore awards 200MW of data centre capacity across four existing operators
article:
Singapore has provisionally allocated 50 megawatts (MW) each to Digital Realty, Equinix, Keppel Data Centres and ST Telemedia Global Data Centres (STT GDC) under its latest data centre application exercise.

The Economic Development Board (EDB) and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) selected the four from more than 20 proposals submitted by local and global players under the second Data Centre Call for Application (DC-CFA2), which opened on 1 December 2025.

All four sites will be on Jurong Island, where JTC is developing a low-carbon data centre park designed to tap low-carbon technologies already available on the island.

Each operator has committed to draw more than half its capacity from green energy, above the minimum set by the exercise. Eligible sources include biomethane, low-carbon ammonia, low-carbon hydrogen and solar panels built into building facades.

Selected operators have also committed to liquid cooling, which circulates fluid rather than blown air to carry heat off computing equipment, and to 100% energy-efficient IT equipment. The facilities are to meet Green Mark for Data Centres Platinum certification.

EDB and IMDA say bids were judged on strategic, economic, and sustainability grounds. Winning proposals anchored advanced computing for uses such as AI in Singapore, promised economic contributions beyond the data centre spending itself, including research collaborations with Singapore-based partners, and met the energy and efficiency commitments.

See also: DayOne secures $530 million green loan from DBS, OCBC and UOB

Equinix describes the award as an extension of its existing partnership with the government. "This award enables us to deepen that commitment, investing in the infrastructure and interconnection needed to bring together AI, cloud, networks, enterprises, and data," says Yee May Leong, managing director of Equinix Singapore.

Similarly, STT GDC’s proposed facility will support advanced computing and AI workloads. Bruno Lopez, its president and group chief executive officer, adds: “Beyond capacity, we will work with customers, technology partners, research institutions and the wider ecosystem to translate this investment into enduring economic value for Singapore, strengthen its digital ecosystem and international connectivity, and support the continued growth and vibrancy of its digital economy. We will pursue these ambitions responsibly, through advanced infrastructure that advances Singapore’s sustainability goals while enabling the next generation of AI and digital innovation.”

EDB and IMDA will review the need for another call for applications in 18 to 24 months.

title: Eurozone business activity up slightly in August on manufacturing surge
article:
(Aug 21): Private-sector activity in the euro area unexpectedly improved slightly in August, thanks to the strongest manufacturing growth in more than four years.

The Composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) compiled by S&P Global rose to 52.1 from 52 in July, staying well above the 50 threshold separating growth from contraction. Analysts in a Bloomberg survey had expected a slight decline to 51.7.

The region’s two largest economies both fell short of estimates, indicating that other parts of the region were behind Friday’s positive surprise. While Germany stayed well above the growth threshold, France sank deeper into contraction.

“The manufacturing sector is again the star performer,” Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said in a statement. As well as precautionary stock building, “there are also encouraging signs of rising demand for AI-related tech goods and rising equipment demand thanks to higher defence spending, notably helping Germany in particular achieve increasingly impressive production gains.”

The 21-nation economy is defying the headwinds created by the Middle East conflict, brushing aside rising energy costs and shaky confidence with surprising strength. Second-quarter output grew 0.4%, stronger than expected.

See also: French business activity unexpectedly weakens on heat wave

Whether such a performance can continue hinges mainly on how the situation between Washington and Tehran evolves. The full effect of the initial energy shock “has yet to play out,” the European Central Bank (ECB) warned last month.

Officials in Frankfurt are weighing the need for another interest-rate hike to curb consumer-price gains following June’s quarter-point increase. Inflation picked up slightly in July, to 2.9%, moving further away from the ECB’s 2% target.

See also: How AI could reinforce dollar dominance

According to S&P Global, price pressures showed signs of further easing in August, for both services and goods.

“However, with the flash PMI signalling solid third quarter GDP growth, a return to hiring by companies for the first time this year, and inflation remaining elevated by historical standards, a hawkish bias is likely to be maintained and further imminent rate hikes cannot be ruled out,” Williamson said.

PMIs are closely watched by markets as they arrive early in the month and are good at revealing trends and turning points in an economy. A measure of breadth of changes in output rather than depth, business surveys can sometimes be difficult to map directly to quarterly GDP.

title: Nvidia in talks for potential tie-up with Korean chip startup Rebellions — Bloomberg
article:
(Aug 21): Nvidia Corp is in early discussions with the Korean artificial intelligence (AI) chip designer Rebellions about possible collaborations, including a technical partnership, an investment or perhaps even an acquisition, according to people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang met with Rebellions co-founder and CEO Sunghyun Park and discussed a potential tie-up at the US company’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California this week, said the people, who asked not to be identified as the information is not public. Huang has led a far-reaching investment spree in recent years, as Nvidia works to maintain its central role in the AI era.

Those deals have included high-profile startups. In late 2025, Nvidia struck an unconventional deal with US AI firm Groq, securing a non-exclusive licence while absorbing most of its engineering talent. Nvidia said it wasn’t an acquisition because Groq continues to operate separately and run its cloud business independently.

Bundang, South Korea-based Rebellions has raised roughly US$850 million from investors including SK Hynix Inc, Samsung Ventures and Arm Holdings plc, and was most recently valued at around US$2.3 billion. It has also secured a direct investment from the Korean government.

Deliberations between Nvidia and six-year-old Rebellions are preliminary and may not lead to a transaction, the people said. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. A representative for Rebellions declined to comment.

Founded in the midst of the pandemic in 2020, Rebellions is among a group of semiconductor startups designing and deploying their own chips to rival market leader Nvidia. The company specialises in neural processing units for data centres, optimised for AI inference work. Less intensive in processing requirements than AI training, inference is the larger-in-volume workload required to operate AI services at scale.

See also: Samsung planning to return up to US$79 bil to shareholders — Bloomberg

Nvidia holds such a dominant share of the semiconductors used to train AI models like those from OpenAI and Anthropic PBC that it has to be wary of antitrust scrutiny. Large acquisitions in the tech industry typically need clearance from authorities such as the US Department of Justice.

An acquisition-like arrangement may also invite regulatory scrutiny from the government in Korea, where semiconductors are viewed as critical strategic assets. Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix are leading manufacturers of memory chips, and work closely with the Korean government on new investment projects.

title: French business activity unexpectedly weakens on heat wave
article:
(Aug 21): France’s private sector unexpectedly weakened this month as extreme summer temperatures took a toll on the services sector.

S&P Global’s Composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) declined to 48.8 in August from 49.4 the previous month — remaining below the 50 mark separating expansion from contraction for an eighth month. Analysts polled by Bloomberg had anticipated a small increase to 49.5.

Services retreated more than anticipated, to 48.4. Manufacturing, by contrast, jumped back into growth territory, with inflation in the goods-producing sector remaining on a downward trajectory.

“The flash PMI report revealed another month of frail economic conditions, with some firms, mainly in the service sector, highlighting the extreme heat as a reason for lower activity and demand,” Joe Hayes, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said on Friday in a statement. “There was some renewed vigour in the manufacturing sector, however, as production rose for the first time since April’s stockpile-driven boost.”

France’s economy has recovered from an early-year wobble to register growth of 0.2% in the second quarter, a pace the central bank reckons will be matched in the third. But that prediction relies in part on strength in the services sector, which Friday’s surveys throw into doubt.

See also: How AI could reinforce dollar dominance

Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou, meanwhile, has blamed heat waves and the Iran war for an advance in the unemployment rate to 8.3%, the highest in almost six years. A further headwind is likely to come in the form of tighter monetary policy, with markets expecting another hike in interest rates from the European Central Bank in September.

The longstanding issue of France’s strained public finances is set to return, too, as the country’s minority government tries to push a cost-cutting budget through a fractured parliament.

PMIs are closely watched by markets as they arrive early in the month and are good at revealing trends and turning points in an economy. A measure of breadth of changes in output rather than depth, business surveys can sometimes be difficult to map directly to quarterly GDP.

See also: Trump’s new tariffs are an opportunity to fight back

Eurozone PMI data will arrive later on Friday.

A separate indicator of business confidence from French statistics agency Insee rose one point to 98 in August, marking the third consecutive month of improvement. The services and retail sectors continued to pick up while the closely watched gauge for industry rose two points to 103 — the highest level since January. The long-term average for the measures is 100.
